scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: A 3D printer can make a toy, a phone stand, even a spare part, out of a spool of plastic. How?

scenes.name: model
scenes.text: It starts with a 3D model on a computer. Slicer software cuts it into hundreds of thin horizontal layers.

scenes.name: melt
scenes.text: The most common printers push a plastic filament into a hot nozzle, around two hundred degrees, so it melts.

scenes.name: draw
scenes.text: The nozzle moves around, squeezing out a thin line of melted plastic, tracing the shape of one layer.

scenes.name: stack
scenes.text: Then it moves up by a fraction of a millimetre, and draws the next layer on top. Each one fuses to the one below.

scenes.name: infill
scenes.text: Inside, it often prints a honeycomb-like pattern instead of solid plastic, to save material. Overhangs get temporary supports.

scenes.name: time
scenes.text: Because it's layer by layer, even small objects can take a few hours to print.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Model, slice, melt, stack. Building from nothing. Follow for more on how things really work.
